extracted.intended_audience: attorneys practicing trademark law before the USPTO (including those sponsoring USPTO.gov accounts for support staff or representing foreign-domiciled clients)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations governing attorney conduct in USPTO trademark practice, including account sponsorship, signature requirements, supervision/monitoring duties, prohibitions on false filings, and possible disciplinary sanctions. Emphasizes rules applicable to representing foreign-domiciled applicants and use of USPTO.gov accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule — representation of foreign-domiciled applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective August 3, 2019, any foreign-domiciled trademark applicant or registrant must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice in the United States. (37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations; improve accuracy of submissions; safeguard integrity of the U.S. trademark register. Practitioners serving as U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled clients are subject to USPTO disciplinary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO.gov account individual-responsibility rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration for, and use of, a USPTO.gov account is limited to the individual to whom the account is registered, and the registered individual is responsible for all activities occurring under that account and any sponsored accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account holders are bound by Terms of Use and the Trademark Verified USPTO.gov Account Agreement. Account credentials must not be shared. Use of an account to submit/alter information exceeding one's authority may breach Terms of Use and violate other USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sharing account credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO.gov account holders are not permitted to share their account credentials with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing credentials can lead to improper filings and disciplinary consequences; account holders remain responsible for activities under their accounts and any sponsored accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on sponsoring support staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys may sponsor USPTO.gov accounts for a reasonable number of support staff only if those staff are (a) directly employed or retained by the attorney/company/firm and (b) work under the attorney's supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsoring attorneys must not attempt to sponsor unauthorized individuals (foreign or domestic companies, groups, clients, agents, attorneys, or other practitioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to take reasonable steps regarding sponsored accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsoring attorneys agree to take reasonable steps to ensure that the support staff's access and use of USPTO systems is consistent with the tasks assigned to them and to immediately remove sponsorship for any individual who has knowingly submitted false signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable steps include vetting/screening and monitoring; failure to do so can support findings of incompetence, lack of diligence, or conduct prejudicial to integrity of the trademark system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature rules for trademark documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark signature rules require: (a) all signatures be signed by a proper person; (b) trademark documents be personally signed by the signatory named on the document; and (c) an electronic signatory must personally enter their adopted signature between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block. (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a),(c),(e); 11.18(a); TMEP §611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may not delegate authority to sign, and document-signing software may not be used to enter or electronically generate someone else's signature. These signature requirements are substantive, not merely technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper execution consequence — unauthorized signatures invalidate support for registration
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark submission signed by a person other than the named signatory is improperly executed and cannot be relied upon to support registration; signatures that fail to meet 'personally signed' or 'personally entered' requirements may jeopardize validity or subject the registration to cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Yusha Zhang; Ex parte Hipkins; In re Cowan; In re Dermahose. The USPTO treats these as substantive defects that can invalidate registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1). This includes false or misleading domicile information, attorney information, signatory information (e.g., where named signatory did not personally enter signature), applicant information, or claims of use (or intent to use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting without undertaking a reasonable inquiry into the factual basis, without evidentiary support, or coupled with other Terms of Use violations constitutes an improper purpose and violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of USPTO systems exceeding authority may violate multiple rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a USPTO.gov account to submit, access, or alter information exceeding one's authority not only breaches the Terms of Use, but may also violate other USPTO Rules including 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(f) and 11.18(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle applies both to primary account holders and to sponsored accounts; account holders are responsible for activities under their accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory obligation over non-attorneys/support staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys who sponsor accounts or supervise staff have an obligation to adequately supervise non-attorneys and ensure compliance with USPTO rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to adequately supervise support staff (including sponsoring unauthorized persons) has been the basis for discipline in multiple USPTO orders; supervisory failures can implicate competence and diligence rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of practitioner knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO in trademark matters are reasonably expected to know (a) applicable trademark prosecution and signature rules, (b) provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by such representation, and (c) potential disciplinary consequences when those provisions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO provides ample guidance (TMEP, webinars, rulemaking notices) and prior disciplinary decisions accessible via the OED Reading Room; lack of knowledge is not an adequate excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended monitoring/search procedure for detecting unauthorized filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys who sponsor USPTO.gov accounts should regularly and frequently search the USPTO's online trademark search system for applications naming them as attorney of record using the search phrase: AT: firstname AND AT: lastname AND FD: (YYYYMMDD TO YYYYMMDD) and compare search results to the attorney's list of actual application filings to find unauthorized filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unauthorized filings are found, the attorney should promptly inform the USPTO via TMScams@uspto.gov. The Final Order here specifies weekly searches while on probation and quarterly reporting to OED (see separate probation obligations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity verification requirement for sponsored accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO rulemaking (Requiring Identity Verification for Attorney-Sponsored Accounts, 88 Fed. Reg. 60667) made identity verification for support staff available Oct. 14, 2023 and required identity verification for all support staff users beginning Jan. 20, 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsoring attorneys are expected to comply with identity verification requirements and should not sponsor individuals to circumvent those processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by sponsoring unauthorized accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsoring unauthorized individuals and failing to monitor sponsored accounts can violate USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct, including 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 (competent representation), § 11.103 (reasonable diligence), and § 11.804(d) (conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the trademark system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order cites these specific provisions as the legal bases for discipline in the presented facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting, monitoring, and affirmative obligations imposed as sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions imposed may include reprimand, probation with conditions, cooperation with inquiries, mandatory monitoring/searches, reporting obligations, and possible suspension if probation requirements are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sanctions in this Final Order: reprimand; twelve (12) months probation; full cooperation with USPTO inquiries into improper filings; weekly searches of TM system while on probation and prompt written notification to Trademark Examination Policy of unauthorized filings; quarterly written reports to OED (every three months) confirming searches and reporting results; potential 30-day immediate suspension procedure upon failure to comply; publication of the Final Order and notice in the Official Gazette.
